questions.q: A Miller-Abrahams hop goes uphill by dE > 0 over distance r. Its rate is
questions.why: MA rates are asymmetric: downhill hops pay only the tunnelling factor exp(-2 alpha r), uphill hops also pay the full Boltzmann factor exp(-dE/kT). The exp(-dE/2kT) form is the symmetric variant and the last option is Marcus theory.

questions.q: Which relation must every rate model in orchid.rates satisfy so that equilibrium is the Fermi-Dirac/Boltzmann state?
questions.why: Detailed balance, W_ij/W_ji = exp(-(E_j-E_i)/kT), guarantees that the equilibrium occupation is Boltzmann (or Fermi-Dirac with exclusion). V11 checks it to 7e-15 for MA, Marcus and MLJ.

questions.q: In Marcus theory, what happens to the rate as the driving force -dE grows beyond the reorganisation energy lambda?
options: It saturates at 2 pi J^2 / hbar
questions.why: The Marcus rate is proportional to exp(-(dE+lambda)^2/(4 lambda kT)). It peaks at -dE = lambda and falls again beyond that: this is the inverted region. Miller-Abrahams has no such regime.

questions.q: The dimensionless disorder sigma-hat used throughout ORCHID is defined as
questions.why: sigma-hat = sigma/kT. Most GDM/EGDM results (for example ln mu ~ -c sigma-hat^2) are written in terms of it.

questions.q: How do the Förster and Dexter exciton transfer rates fall off with distance r?
options: Förster as r^-6, Dexter as exp(-2r/L)
Förster as exp(-2r/L), Dexter as r^-6
questions.why: Förster transfer is dipole-dipole coupling, so k = (1/tau)(R0/r)^6. Dexter transfer is an electron-exchange process that needs orbital overlap, so it decays exponentially with distance.

02.title: Kinetic Monte Carlo: mobility, TOF and relaxation

questions.q: In the BKL/Gillespie algorithm, the time step after an event is drawn as
questions.why: The waiting time of a Poisson process with total rate R_tot is exponentially distributed. Sampling it by inversion gives dt = -ln(u)/R_tot. The event itself is chosen with probability W_i/R_tot.

questions.q: What does the Fenwick tree in orchid._fenwick buy for interacting KMC with n events?
options: O(log n) selection and O(log n) update
questions.why: A binary indexed tree keeps prefix sums, so event selection and the local rate updates both cost O(log n). V16/R11 measure a 27-135x speed-up over the dense O(n) engine.

questions.q: At low density and long times, the mean energy of carriers in a Gaussian DOS of width sigma relaxes to
questions.why: The occupied DOS is the Gaussian multiplied by the Boltzmann factor, which is again a Gaussian, centred at -sigma^2/kT (Bässler 1993). V4 recovers this to 1.7 % at sigma-hat = 2.

questions.q: A time-of-flight transient becomes dispersive when disorder increases. What do you see?
options: The plateau tilts and the post-transit tail broadens
A flat plateau and a sharp drop
No transit time can be defined
questions.why: Dispersive (Scher-Montroll-like) transport shows a current that already decays before t_tr and a long tail after it. The transit time is then taken from the intersection of the log-log asymptotes (V10).

questions.q: How is the drift mobility obtained from an independent-carrier KMC run?
options: mu = <x(t)>/(F t), the mean drift displacement per unit field and time
questions.why: The carriers are driven by a field F along x. The mean drift velocity is <x>/t, and mu = v/F. Reduced fields eFa much smaller than sigma keep the run in the linear-response regime.

questions.q: In linear response, the master equation maps onto which problem?
options: A random walk with absorbing boundaries
A resistor network with conductances G_ij proportional to W_ij f_i (1 - f_j)
questions.why: Linearising the steady-state ME around equilibrium gives Kirchhoff's laws on a network with conductances (e^2/kT) W_ij f_i (1-f_j). ORCHID solves it with CG, preconditioned by Jacobi or AMG.

questions.q: What causes the density enhancement g1(p) of the EGDM?
options: Filling of deep tail states, which raises the effective transport level
questions.why: Extra carriers first fill the deepest states. The remaining carriers sit higher in the DOS and need less activation, so mu rises steeply once p is above about 1e-4 per site (V2).

questions.q: In Pasveer's parametrisation mu0(T) = mu_00 exp(-c2 sigma-hat^2), c2 is approximately
questions.why: Pasveer et al. (PRL 2005) fitted c1 = 1.8e-9 and c2 = 0.42 for the 3D lattice with alpha = 10/a. ORCHID's own fit gives c2 = 0.36 (V1). The difference comes from the finite lattice and the hopping range.

questions.q: Why is the ME much cheaper than KMC for the zero-field mobility?
options: It runs on the GPU only
It solves one sparse linear system and has no stochastic noise
questions.why: One CG solve gives the exact ensemble mean for that disorder realisation, whereas KMC must average very long trajectories. V1 shows that the two agree to 3 % where both apply.

questions.q: For a Gaussian DOS at high density, the generalised Einstein ratio g3 = eD/(mu kT) is
questions.why: g3 = (n/kT)(dE_F/dn). For a degenerate (state-filling) Gaussian DOS this exceeds 1, and the drift-diffusion code must include it (R05; see van Mensfoort and Coehoorn).

04.title: Drift-diffusion: diodes, solar cells and OLEDs

questions.q: Why is the Scharfetter-Gummel discretisation used for the current between two nodes?
options: It is second-order accurate in h
It uses the exact exponential solution of J between nodes, so it stays stable for large potential steps
questions.why: SG integrates J = q mu n F + q D n' exactly for a constant field between the nodes. The result contains Bernoulli functions B(dpsi/kT) and avoids the oscillations of central differences.

questions.q: The trap-free space-charge-limited current (Mott-Gurney) is
options: J = q n mu V / L
questions.why: Mott-Gurney: J = 9 eps mu V^2/(8 L^3). V5 approaches it (ratio 1.06 at 40 V) once diffusion and the built-in voltage become negligible.

questions.q: Koster et al. (2005) predict that Voc depends on the light intensity (generation G) as
options: dVoc/dln G = kT/e for bimolecular (Langevin) recombination
questions.why: With bimolecular recombination, Voc = Eg/e - (kT/e) ln((1-P)gamma Nc^2/(P G)). The slope is kT/e. ORCHID reproduces it with a slope of 1.004 kT/e and deviations of at most 1.3 mV (V6).

questions.q: The Langevin recombination coefficient is
questions.why: Langevin: gamma_L = q(mu_n+mu_p)/(eps0 eps_r). ``langevin_prefactor`` scales it for reduced recombination.

questions.q: For the metal-insulator-metal picture used in Device, with injection barriers phi_a and phi_c, the built-in voltage is
questions.why: The difference between the electrode work functions equals the gap minus the two injection barriers. Below Vbi the dark current is diffusion-limited, above it the current becomes drift/SCLC-limited.

questions.q: Photo-CELIV extracts the mobility (Juska et al. 2000, small-charge limit) from
questions.why: With a ramp of slope A, the extraction peak t_max gives mu = 2d^2/(3A t_max^2) (plus a correction for dj/j0). V17 shows that the extracted mu converges to the input mu once qA t_max >> kT.

questions.q: The low-frequency capacitance of a trap-free single-carrier SCLC diode is
questions.why: Space charge makes the small-signal response lag the transit, so C(0) = 3/4 eps/L (Martens). V19 obtains 0.76-0.77 and a peak at f tau_dc = 0.72.

questions.q: What does a small-perturbation transient photovoltage (TPV) measure?
options: The lifetime of the excess carriers at open circuit
questions.why: A weak light pulse at Voc raises the carrier density a little. The decay of Voc gives the small-signal recombination lifetime. In thin devices this differs from the bulk 1/(2 gamma n) because of electrode charge (V17).

questions.q: IMPS modulates ____ and measures ____.
options: light intensity; photocurrent at short circuit
questions.why: IMPS is the photocurrent transfer function at short circuit. IMVS is the photovoltage version at open circuit.

questions.q: The dc transit time of a trap-free SCLC diode is
questions.why: The field grows across an SCLC device, and integrating dx/(mu F) gives tau_dc = (4/3) L^2/(mu V). This is the time scale for the admittance analysis.

questions.q: In the gradual-channel model, the linear-regime drain current per unit width is
questions.why: For |V_D| << |V_G - V_T| the channel is a uniform sheet of charge C_i(V_G-V_T), so I/W = mu C_i (V_G-V_T) V_D / L.

questions.q: In saturation, the gradual-channel current is
questions.why: Beyond pinch-off, I_sat/W = mu C_i (V_G-V_T)^2/(2L). The saturation mobility is extracted from the slope of sqrt(I_D) against V_G.

questions.q: Why does an OFET need a 2D solver?
options: The field has strong lateral and vertical components, and the accumulation layer is a few nm thick
questions.why: The gate field confines charge vertically while the drain field drives it laterally. The contacts are 2D boundaries. Dd2d solves the coupled Poisson/continuity equations on an (x, y) grid.

questions.q: What does the 15-colour Jacobian in dd2d do?
options: It perturbs structurally independent unknowns together, so building the finite-difference Jacobian costs 15 residual evaluations instead of N
questions.why: Unknowns whose stencils do not overlap can be perturbed at the same time. Graph colouring reduces the cost of the sparse Jacobian to one residual evaluation per colour.

questions.q: V23 compares the 2D DD OFET with
options: The gradual-channel model with the input mobility
questions.why: The mobilities extracted from the simulated transfer curves reproduce the input mobility: 0.97x in the linear regime and 1.06x in saturation.

07.title: Optics: transfer matrices, generation and outcoupling

questions.q: The transfer-matrix method assumes
options: Coherent plane waves in planar layers, with interface and propagation matrices
questions.why: Each interface (Fresnel coefficients) and each layer (phase exp(i k d)) is a 2x2 matrix. The product gives the field everywhere. ORCHID agrees with the independent tmm package to 1e-15 (V15).

questions.q: The local absorption that sets the exciton generation rate is proportional to
questions.why: Absorbed power density is (1/2) omega eps0 Im(eps) |E|^2 = omega eps0 n k |E|^2. Dividing by the photon energy and integrating over the AM1.5G spectrum gives G(x).

questions.q: For any lossless check of an optics solver, which identity must hold?
questions.why: Energy conservation. V8 checks the Airy formula to 1e-16 and R+T+A=1 to 1e-5 for absorbing stacks.

questions.q: The classical ray-optics estimate of OLED outcoupling into air is
questions.why: With isotropic emission inside a medium of index n, only the escape cone sin(theta) < 1/n gets out: eta ~ 1/(2n^2), about 20 % for n = 1.7. The dipole model (R20) refines this.

questions.q: Near a metal mirror, a dipole's decay rate oscillates with distance and is strongly enhanced at very short distances. Why?
options: Interference with its reflected field (CPS); near-field coupling to surface plasmons and lossy waves
questions.why: The Chance-Prock-Silbey theory gives the oscillation from interference and the short-distance quenching from evanescent coupling into the metal. ORCHID reproduces the perfect-mirror formulas to 8e-4 (V20).

questions.q: In 3D, the exciton diffusion coefficient from KMC rates k_j to neighbours at r_j is
questions.why: <r^2> = 6 D t in 3D, and each hop adds r_j^2 at rate k_j. V7 confirms this within statistical error.

questions.q: The exciton diffusion length is
questions.why: L_D = sqrt(D tau) by convention, which is the 1D RMS displacement. Some papers quote sqrt(6 D tau) for the 3D displacement, so always check the definition.

questions.q: At high exciton density, triplet-triplet annihilation adds which loss term to the continuity equation?
questions.why: TTA is bimolecular. V18 checks that the KMC loss rate divided by n^2 is constant (5 % spread), so the continuum gamma_TT is well defined.

questions.q: For a purely fluorescent emitter, spin statistics limit the singlet fraction to
questions.why: Electron-hole recombination produces singlets and triplets in a 1:3 ratio. Phosphorescent or TADF emitters can harvest the triplets as well (eta_ST = 1).

questions.q: Why does EQE roll off at high current in OLEDs?
options: Bimolecular quenching (TTA, exciton-polaron quenching TPQ) grows faster than the generation
questions.why: Loss channels proportional to n^2 (TTA) or n*p (TPQ) grow faster than the linear radiative channel, so the quantum efficiency falls as J rises.

questions.q: How does the device KMC compute the current with low noise?
options: By counting carriers that reach the electrodes
Ramo-Shockley: every hop contributes e q dz/(L A)
questions.why: Every displacement induces charge on the electrodes, so all hops contribute. This converges much faster than counting only the extracted carriers.

questions.q: The image charge in the electrode makes a carrier near the contact
options: Lower in energy, which lowers the injection barrier
questions.why: The image attraction -e^2/(16 pi eps z) lowers the barrier near the electrode. This is Schottky barrier lowering, and it strongly affects injection-limited currents.

questions.q: Why are electrostatics split into a mean-field sheet part and an exact short-range part?
options: The sheet part is more accurate
Exact long-range Coulomb sums are too expensive. Sheets give the long-range part cheaply, and close pairs are treated exactly.
questions.why: The 1D sheet Green's function updates in O(Lz) per event. The exact screened Coulomb within r_coul minus its sheet part makes the sum converge to full Coulomb as r_coul grows.

questions.q: What changed for exciton-polaron quenching in v0.4 (CoupledDeviceKMC)?
options: TPQ is evaluated against the live polaron positions in the same event loop, not against a frozen configuration
questions.why: In v0.3, excitons saw a polaron snapshot drawn from the mean density profile. Now charges and excitons share one clock and two Fenwick trees, so all correlations are kept (R24).

questions.q: Which exact identity does V24 check in every coupled run?
options: formed + alive_start = radiative + non-radiative + TPQ + TTA + overflow + alive_end
questions.why: Every exciton that exists during the measurement must end in exactly one channel or still be alive at the end. V24 finds an imbalance of exactly 0 in all runs.

10.title: Morphology, DFT couplings and MD trajectories

questions.q: For a symmetric dimer, DIPRO's effective transfer integral equals
questions.why: For identical monomers with zero site-energy difference, the bonding/antibonding splitting is 2|J|. V21 checks this to 0.24 % with HF/STO-3G in PySCF.

questions.q: Why must molecules be made whole across periodic boundaries before computing centres of mass?
options: A molecule split by the boundary would otherwise get its centre somewhere in the middle of the box
questions.why: molecule_centres unwraps every atom by the minimum image relative to the first atom of its molecule. V26 places 397 boundary-straddling molecules and recovers the centres exactly.

questions.q: Dipolar disorder produces site energies that are
options: Always zero on average with zero width
Spatially correlated, which extends the sqrt(F) Poole-Frenkel-like regime
questions.why: Each site energy is a sum over many nearby dipoles, so neighbouring sites share most of the sum. This is the correlated disorder model (CDM, Novikov).

questions.q: The transfer integral between molecules typically decays with distance as
questions.why: Orbital overlap decays exponentially. V21 extracts beta = 2.9 per Angstrom for cofacial ethylene.

questions.q: What does V26 prove about the graph solver?
options: Mobility does not depend on morphology
A lattice-shaped 'trajectory' imported through molecule_centres gives the same ME mobility as the Lattice solver to 3e-14
questions.why: This exact equivalence shows that the import -> MolecularGraph -> master equation pipeline adds no error, so differences on real morphologies are physical.

11.title: Exhaustive search, ML surrogates and Bayesian inversion

questions.q: A full grid with n points per parameter in d dimensions needs
questions.why: This exponential cost is why zoom_search refines the grid around the best point level by level, and why surrogates help for expensive models.

questions.q: Why does ORCHID fit mobility data with log-RMSE?
options: Mobility spans many decades, so relative (log) errors weight all points fairly
questions.why: On a linear scale the largest-mobility points would dominate the fit. The log metric treats a factor of 2 equally everywhere.

questions.q: A Gaussian-process surrogate provides
options: A predictive mean and an uncertainty; hyperparameters set by maximising the marginal likelihood
questions.why: The GP posterior gives mean and variance. GPSurrogate.fit grid-searches length scale, signal and noise using the log marginal likelihood.

questions.q: V22 reports '3/3 covered'. What does that mean?
options: The true parameters lie inside the 95 % credible intervals for all three parameters
questions.why: This is a calibration check of the Bayesian inversion: the synthetic ground truth must fall inside the reported intervals.

questions.q: Latin hypercube sampling ensures that
options: All points lie on a grid
Each parameter's range is stratified, one sample per stratum
questions.why: LHS spreads n samples so that every one-dimensional projection is evenly covered. It is a good design for training surrogates.

12.title: Massive parallelism: MPI, threads, GPU and sublattice KMC

questions.q: Why is independent-carrier KMC ideal for GPUs?
options: Walkers do not interact, so each GPU thread can propagate one walker
questions.why: Embarrassingly parallel. orchid.gpu.kmc_independent_gpu launches one CUDA thread per walker.

questions.q: In the synchronous-sublattice algorithm, blocks of the same sublattice can be updated in parallel because
options: They are separated by at least the interaction range, so their events are independent within a window
questions.why: Blocks of side B >= 2 r_c in an 8-colour checkerboard never share hops or neighbours within one window (Shim and Amar 2005).

questions.q: How does v0.4 remove the time-window bias of sublattice KMC?
options: By running several windows tau and extrapolating mu(tau) to tau -> 0
questions.why: mobility_sublattice_extrapolated fits mu(tau) with a polynomial in tau. V25 reduces the error from about 5 % (single window) to about 1 %.

questions.q: ORCHID's MPI task farm reproduces the serial result bit-for-bit because
options: Random seeds are attached to tasks, not to ranks
questions.why: Each task carries its own seed, so the decomposition over ranks cannot change any random stream. V16 checks this.

questions.q: Amdahl's law: if a fraction s of the runtime is serial, the speed-up on P cores is at most
questions.why: The serial part does not shrink. This is why ORCHID parallelises the outermost loop (ensembles, sweeps) as well as the inner kernels.

questions.q: Why does V15 compare against NIST Sesame on identical grids?
options: Identical inputs isolate the equations and discretisation, so agreement to 1e-6 shows both codes solve the same problem
questions.why: With the same mesh and parameters, any remaining difference comes from the model or the discretisation, not from resolution.

questions.q: When a benchmark fails, what does validation/criteria.py say to do?
options: Fix the code; tolerances are set in advance
questions.why: Tolerances come from the published references and are fixed before running. Loosening them after the fact would make the benchmark meaningless.

questions.q: How should a stochastic KMC result be compared to an exact value?
questions.why: KMC estimates have statistical error. V7 and V24 use z-scores: 1.4 sigma for D and well within 3 sigma for eta_rad.

questions.q: V27 records events per second and solve times. What is it for?
options: Detecting performance regressions on the same machine across versions
questions.why: Throughput depends on the hardware, so V27 is recorded rather than graded, together with CPU count and library versions.

questions.q: Which command re-runs every benchmark and rewrites BENCHMARKS.md?
questions.why: Without --run it only re-evaluates existing results. With IDs (for example --run V24 V25) it re-runs only those benchmarks.
